subject: Ambassador egress capacity model and per-tenant headroom for AcmeAI private pool
messages:
From: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Danielle Park <danielle@cloudinfra.io>, ops@acme-ai.com
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 8 May 2029 14:12:00 +0000
Subject: Ambassador egress capacity model and per-tenant headroom for AcmeAI private pool

Danielle / Acme ops team —

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. Per our discussion, I put together a lightweight egress-and-proxy sizing model that focuses on the Ambassador (edge) layer behavior when AcmeAI runs a private VPC deployment behind their transit gateway. High-level asks from our side: confirm expected request QPS distribution, TLS termination plan (Ambassador vs customer-managed LB), and whether tenant isolation will be enforced at L7 (route-level) or via separate hostnames.

Key assumptions in the attached workbook:
- Peak sustained inference QPS: 18,000 requests/s across all tenants (sustained 10m window)
- Average response payload (compressed JSON): 2.5 KB (model tokens already stripped at runtime)
- TLS terminated at Ambassador (recommended): adds ~200 µs extra CPU per request on common HW; enabling TLS passthrough reduces CPU but increases connection count and limits routing flexibility
- HTTP/2 multiplexing used for long-lived connections between clients and Ambassador; backend connections to inference nodes use persistent HTTP/1.1 or gRPC depending on your stack

Initial capacity outputs:
- Raw egress bandwidth at peak: 18k * 2.5 KB * 1.2 (headers+overhead) ≈ 54 MB/s ≈ 430 Mbps
- Add 30% headroom for cache/KV warmups and bursty artifact fetches → 559 Mbps recommended
- Control-plane (webhooks, health checks) adds ~40 Mbps on median day; plan for 650 Mbps soft ceiling per Ambassador cluster

Operational considerations that affect sizing:
1) Multiplexing contention: With HTTP/2 clients, a single Ambassador CPU core can handle many concurrent streams, but CPU utilization can spike if TLS ciphers or body parsing are heavy. We recommend limiting streams per connection and using connection pooling to backends.
2) TLS acceleration: If Acme will enable hardware TLS offload on their edge router, we can reduce Ambassador host CPU and therefore right-size fewer hosts — the model includes a toggle.
3) Tenant isolation: If you want hard egress guarantees per tenant, we suggest dedicated Ambassador workers per high-commit tenant (e.g., top 3 customers). Otherwise, use token-aware routing with soft RBW (rate bandwidth) limits.

Ask: can you confirm the per-tenant 95th percentile sustained QPS for the three largest tenants? I used provisional numbers in sheet tab "tenant_breakdown". Also please confirm if your egress topology uses private NATs with 1:64 port multiplexing (common in our partners).

Next steps I propose:
- Acme confirms tenant QPS and TLS plan (deadline Thu 9 May EOD)
- Jonas and I will run a micro-benchmark of Ambassador CPU + TLS on our staging hardware with your payload sample (target: Thu evening PST)
- We finalize the Ambassador cluster sizing and export a minimal ops runbook for failover and warmup behavior by Friday

Attachments: ambassador-egress-bandwidth-model.xlsx (sheet notes included) and topology PNG.

Thanks —
Laura
Laura Bennett
Head, Private Deployments — Redwood Inference

From: Danielle Park <danielle@cloudinfra.io>

Date: Wed, 8 May 2029 19:03:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Ambassador egress capacity model and per-tenant headroom for AcmeAI private pool

Laura —

Appreciate the detailed workbook. Quick clarifications from Acme ops:
- Per-tenant 95th P95 sustained QPS (current production telemetry, last 30d): Tenant A = 7,200 r/s, Tenant B = 4,000 r/s, Tenant C = 1,500 r/s. Remaining tenants lumped = 5,300 r/s.
- TLS termination: we plan to terminate TLS at our edge router (hardware offload) and provide plain HTTP/2 to Ambassador inside the private VPC. That will save CPU headroom on Ambassador hosts.
- NAT topology: we use per-subnet NAT with 1:128 ephemeral port multiplexing (so port exhaustion is less likely).

One ask from our side: can you include a section showing how many concurrent TLS handshakes/sec Ambassador needs to handle if we opt into mutual TLS for tenant identity? We are evaluating mTLS for strong tenant isolation.

We can make the sample payload available via a shared S3 link; I’ll drop that in Ops.

—Danielle
Danielle Park
Cloud Infrastructure Lead, AcmeAI

From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>
To: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Danielle Park <danielle@cloudinfra.io>, ops@acme-ai.com
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 9 May 2029 02:21:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Ambassador egress capacity model and per-tenant headroom for AcmeAI private pool

Thanks for the numbers, Danielle — very useful. I ran the numbers quickly and updated the workbook (tab: "mTLS_and_handshakes"). Highlights below:

1) Adjusted raw egress bandwidth (based on tenant breakdown and 2.5 KB avg payload):
- Tenant A: 7,200 * 2.5KB * 1.2 ≈ 20.9 MB/s
- Tenant B: 4,000 * 2.5KB * 1.2 ≈ 11.5 MB/s
- Tenant C: 1,500 * 2.5KB * 1.2 ≈ 4.3 MB/s
- Others: 5,300 * 2.5KB * 1.2 ≈ 15.4 MB/s
- Sum ≈ 52.1 MB/s ≈ 417 Mbps — matches Laura’s earlier baseline after rounding.

2) mTLS handshake load (if enabled):
- If we require full handshake per connection (no session reuse) at 13k handshakes/minute peak (derived from average connection churn), CPU cost on Ambassador increases significantly. However with session resumption and long-lived HTTP/2 streams, handshake rate drops to < 1k/min for same QPS.
- Practical recommendation: require client certs but enable TLS session resumption and set client idle timeout to 15m. This keeps handshake CPU to <10% of a single Ambassador worker at peak for our staging profile.

3) Ambassador worker sizing (staging hardware: 32 vCPU, 64 GB RAM):
- Baseline TLS-terminated worker (no HW TLS offload): 4 workers per cluster to keep 70% CPU at peak (with p95 latency headroom).
- With hardware TLS offload at the edge (your plan): 2 workers per cluster sufficient, primarily for routing and parsing.
- Network egress per worker: assume 200 Mbps NIC allocation to allow healthy headroom and avoid NIC saturation at 75% utilization. So a 4-worker cluster maps to ~800 Mbps NIC budget.

4) Connection count and ephemeral ports:
- With HTTP/2, client connections are long-lived. We estimate ~12k simultaneous client streams mapped across ~1.5k client connections (avg 8 streams/connection). Port multiplexing 1:128 is more than adequate.

Operational recommendations I’ll include in the runbook:
- Warm pools: pre-warm 1 worker per cluster with cached KV and model prefixes to absorb sudden spikes for 2–3 minutes while autoscale adds capacity.
- Canary scaling: scale new worker pools gradually and route 10% traffic initially for 5 minutes before full cutover.
- Fallback: if Ambassador cluster approaches NIC saturation, route low-priority tenants to a degraded-service path with stricter per-tenant rate cap (configurable).

I’ll schedule the microbench tonight using Acme’s sample payload (please confirm upload link). Laura/Vivek, I’ll post results in the Drive link and summarize recommended cluster counts for prod, staging, and DR.

—Jonas
Jonas Weber
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference

Laura
